title: End of Dennard scaling
question: Is the growth rate of clock frequency (doublings per year, per processor) lower from the break year on than before it, while the growth rate of transistor count is not?

issues.text: The data shows when the clock stopped speeding up, not why.
issues.fix: The Dennard step states the mechanism (P ≈ N·C·V²·f with V no longer scaling); supply voltage per processor would test it and is not in this data.

issues.text: The break year is chosen from the same clock data that is then tested, which inflates the evidence.
issues.fix: The breaks step shows the whole SSE curve; the caveats say a sup-F (Andrews) test is the fair one.

issues.text: About 100 processors, chosen by the original authors (mostly Intel/AMD desktop and server parts).
issues.fix: Read it as the frontier of commodity CPUs, not all chips (GPUs and phones are missing).

alternatives.question: Did single-thread performance slow at the same break as the clock?
alternatives.why: Drill down: the reason performance growth slowed.

alternatives.question: Did cores per processor start growing at the break?
alternatives.why: Drill down: where the extra transistors went.

alternatives.question: Did supply voltage stop falling at the same time?
alternatives.why: Expand: the mechanism (Dennard), which needs voltage per processor (e.g. data sheets, Wikipedia's lists of Intel and AMD processors).

hypotheses.statement: Clock frequency grows more slowly (fewer doublings per year) from the break year on than before it.
hypotheses.null: The clock grows at the same rate in both eras (one straight line on the log scale).

hypotheses.statement: Transistor count keeps doubling about every two years after the break.
hypotheses.null: Transistor growth slows at the break as much as the clock does.

concepts.label: Clock frequency
concepts.description: Clock in MHz per processor, as log2.

concepts.label: Year of introduction
concepts.description: Fractional year a processor came out.

concepts.label: Era
concepts.description: Before the break year, or from it on (the break the clock data chose).

concepts.label: Supply voltage
concepts.why: The mechanism: Dennard scaling ended when V stopped falling.

strategy.detail: Processor data sheets or Wikipedia's processor lists (core voltage), matched on processor name and year.

data.request: Core supply voltage per desktop/server processor, 1990–2022
data.source: Wikipedia lists of Intel and AMD microprocessors; vendor data sheets
data.why: To show V stopped scaling at the same break.

method.summary: Fit log2(value) = a + b·year in each era and compare the slopes b (doublings per year) with their 95% intervals; a Chow F-test compares two lines with one.

steps.title: Parse the five trend files
steps.detail: p_* steps: year and value per processor; points adds log2_value.

steps.title: Find the break
steps.detail: breaks: two-line SSE for every year 1995–2014; best = the minimum.

steps.title: Fit each era
steps.detail: eras: slope, 95% interval, doubling time per measure and era.

steps.title: Chow test
steps.detail: chow: F and p for one line against two, per measure.

steps.title: Compare the slopes
steps.detail: Clock and power slowdown near 0 against transistors near 1.

caveats: The break year is fitted on the clock data, so the Chow p for frequency is optimistic; for transistors it is a fair test of that year.
Pre-2010 points were digitised from a published plot; values carry a few percent of reading error.
Processors are a curated sample of high-end CPUs, mostly Intel and AMD; mobile chips and GPUs follow other curves.
Power is typical TDP, a cooling budget rather than measured power.
Correlation in time: trends with year are not causes; the mechanism (voltage scaling) is not in the data.
